segments: A freelance illustrator whose entire portfolio is an Instagram grid, who has just been asked by a prospective client for "a link to your site"
A newsletter writer or solo product maker who needs a page collecting email addresses before a launch date they have already announced
A one-person studio or VA keeping a dozen-plus tiny one-pagers alive for other people's businesses

business.what_it_does: Simple, free, fully responsive one-page sites for pretty much anything.
business.business_model: freemium subscription — free tier plus paid annual Pro plans

facts.statement: Carrd lets users build up to three sites per account and use all of Carrd's core features for free.

provenance.quote: Build up to three sites per account and use all of Carrd's core features – for free!

facts.statement: Carrd's entry-level paid plan, Pro Lite, costs $9/year and offers improvements over the free Basic experience.

provenance.quote: This is the entry-level Pro plan. At just $9 / year, it offers some nice improvements over the free Basic experience while still being extremely affordable.

facts.statement: Pro Standard costs $19/year and is described as Carrd's most popular Pro plan.

provenance.quote: This is the mid-tier Pro plan. At $19 / year, this is by far the most popular Pro plan in part because it covers a wide range of use cases...

facts.statement: Pro Plus costs $49/year and adds developer-friendly features such as custom forms on top of Pro Standard.

provenance.quote: This is the top-tier Pro plan. At $49 / year, this plan is built for power users as it offers not only the features of Pro Standard, but also more powerful, developer-friendly features like custom forms...

facts.statement: Signup forms, which capture visitor names and emails to third-party email/CRM platforms, require Pro Standard or higher.

provenance.quote: Requires Pro Standard or higher

facts.statement: Signup forms can send captured contacts to over a dozen platforms including ActiveCampaign, beehiiv, Brevo, Mailchimp, HubSpot, Klaviyo, and Sendy.

provenance.quote: Signup forms allow you to capture visitor names and emails to ActiveCampaign contacts, beehiiv publications, Brevo lists, Buttondown subscriber lists, EmailOctopus lists, GetResponse lists, Ghost members, HubSpot contacts, Kit forms, Klaviyo lists, Loops contacts and lists, Mailchimp audiences, MailerLite groups, Mailjet contacts, Omnisend contacts, Resend contacts, Sender subscribers, SendFox lists, SendGrid lists, or Sendy lists.

facts.statement: Carrd sites can be published to custom domains with full SSL support via Let's Encrypt.

provenance.quote: Publish sites to any custom domains you own with full SSL support (via Let's Encrypt).

facts.statement: Carrd launched Carrd Analytics, a native, cookie-free site analytics service with reporting in the dashboard, on October 2, 2026.

provenance.quote: Launched Carrd Analytics, our native, cookie-free site analytics service that requires minimal setup and provides reporting directly within the dashboard

facts.statement: Form-category templates can collect emails and feedback, and can sell products if the account is on a Pro Plus plan or higher.

provenance.quote: Designs built entirely around forms that can collect emails, gather customer feedback, and even sell stuff (if you're on a Pro Plus plan or higher).

facts.statement: New users can test Pro features free for 7 days with no payment or credit card required, and can upgrade to a full Pro plan any time during or after the trial.

provenance.quote: Test drive Pro's top features (like custom domains and advanced forms) free for a full 7 days – no payment or credit card required. Upgrade to a full Pro plan at any time during or after your trial.

facts.statement: Carrd offers starting-point templates grouped into Profile, Landing, Form, Portfolio, and Sectioned categories.

provenance.quote: Or select one of the above categories to narrow things down a bit. You can also choose a blank page if you'd rather start from scratch.

facts.statement: Carrd is aimed at people who need a single-page web presence — a profile, landing page, portfolio, or form — rather than a full multi-page site.

segments.name: A freelance illustrator whose entire portfolio is an Instagram grid, who has just been asked by a prospective client for "a link to your site"
segments.situation: Their shareable identity today is a social profile and a link-in-bio page they do not control the look of: same layout as everyone else, someone else's branding in the footer, and a feed that buries the three pieces of work they actually want seen. They likely own a domain bought during an earlier burst of enthusiasm that still points nowhere. They have probably opened a full site builder at some point and closed it again, because the tool assumed pages they do not have content for — an about page, a blog, a shop — when the whole of their material is one page: a photo, a sentence, six images, and a way to be contacted. Being inferred, the specifics vary, but the shape is consistent: the work exists, the credible place to point someone at it does not, and the gap only becomes urgent when somebody asks.
segments.job_to_be_done: Be taken seriously by the person deciding whether to hire them — one link that reads as theirs, sent back within the hour, rather than "here's my Instagram".
segments.trigger: A client, recruiter or event organiser asks for a website link, or they are given a speaker/contributor bio slot that wants a URL — and the only answer they have is a social handle.

pains.statement: The only link they can send is on a platform that decides how their work is framed, and that carries someone else's name under it.
Carrd positions this buyer as an individual who wants their own site further branded with a custom domain.

provenance.quote: from individuals further branding their sites with [custom domains](/docs/sites/using-a-custom-domain) to businesses using forms to collect email addresses and [customer feedback](/docs/forms/setting-up-a-contact-form)

pains.statement: Conventional site builders are more site than they have content for: they are asked to fill a navigation bar when they have one page of material.
They stall at the point of publishing because a half-finished site feels worse than no site, so the link never gets sent.

segments.name: A newsletter writer or solo product maker who needs a page collecting email addresses before a launch date they have already announced
segments.situation: They have a list somewhere — beehiiv, Kit, Mailchimp, Buttondown — and a date they have told people about. What they do not have is a page worth sending traffic to: right now interested people get pointed at the email provider's own hosted signup form, which looks like the provider and not like the thing being launched, or at a social post that scrolls away. They are also the person who will have to wire the form up, and they are weighing "spend the evening on a landing page" against "spend the evening on the actual product". The specifics here are inferred rather than observed; what is consistent is that the audience exists before the page does, and every day without a page is signups they cannot recover.
segments.job_to_be_done: Stop losing interested people between "this sounds good" and "tell me when it's out" — have somewhere to send attention today, not after a build.
segments.trigger: A launch or publication date gets set and announced publicly, or a post unexpectedly travels and they realise there is nowhere to capture the people reading it.

pains.statement: Carrd describes this buyer as a business using forms to collect email addresses and customer feedback.

provenance.quote: from individuals further branding their sites with [custom domains](/docs/sites/using-a-custom-domain) to businesses using forms to collect email addresses and [customer feedback](/docs/forms/setting-up-a-contact-form)

pains.statement: Attention arrives before infrastructure: interest has to be captured this week, and standing up a page plus a form plus a domain plus SSL is not a this-week job if done by hand.
They do not want a second place to manage subscribers — whatever they build has to deposit names and emails into the list tool they already use.
They may build on the free tier first and only then discover that the signup form is the part that needs a paid plan, which feels like a bait at the exact moment they are trying to ship.

segments.name: A one-person studio or VA keeping a dozen-plus tiny one-pagers alive for other people's businesses
segments.situation: Their portfolio of work is not one site, it is many small ones: a client's event page, a restaurant's hours-and-menu page, a coach's booking page, a band's tour page. Each one needs its own domain, must not carry a builder's badge, and must survive being handed back if the client leaves or decides to manage it themselves. The administrative weight is the problem rather than the design: per-site subscriptions on mainstream builders, separate logins per client, and no clean way to transfer ownership. This situation is inferred from the shape of the product's volume tiers and transfer/sharing features rather than from anything a customer has been recorded saying.
segments.job_to_be_done: Keep many small client sites running for near-nothing per site, and be able to walk away from any one of them cleanly without a migration or an awkward conversation about who owns the login.
segments.trigger: The next client site hits the ceiling of the plan they are on, or a client asks to take their page in-house and they have no mechanism to hand it over.

pains.statement: A three-site allowance stops being relevant the moment the work is client work rather than personal, so the cap is hit almost immediately.
Handover is the sharp edge: without a transfer mechanism, leaving a client means either keeping their site on a personal account forever or rebuilding it somewhere else.
Per-site monthly pricing elsewhere makes a portfolio of small, low-value pages uneconomic to maintain at all.
Every client-facing page carrying a builder's badge in the footer undercuts the impression that the studio built it.

objections.objection: "One page is a dead end. I'll put a weekend into this and then need a second page — an about, a shop, a blog — and have to rebuild the whole thing somewhere else."
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this. The material is explicit that Carrd is a one-page product and there is no supplied evidence of multi-page sites. The only partial mitigation is lock-in, not capability: on Pro Plus the unminified HTML, CSS, JS and images can be downloaded (excluding server-side code), and sites can be transferred to another user, so the work is not trapped — but a reader who knows they will need a second page is not persuaded by this, and the copy should not pretend otherwise.

objections.objection: "I can already put a link in my bio for free, and Carrd's own free tier publishes three sites. So what exactly am I paying for?"
objections.answer: The paid tiers are sold on specific, checkable upgrades rather than on capability in general: a custom domain you own with SSL via Let's Encrypt, no "Made with Carrd" branding in the footer, custom favicons and share images instead of auto screenshots, and — from Pro Standard — forms that deposit signups into an existing email tool. The free tier is real (three sites, all core features) and the paid starting price is $19/year, with Pro Lite at $9/year, so the decision is framed as a once-a-year amount rather than a subscription commitment.

objections.objection: "The thing I actually need will turn out to be on a higher tier. I'll pay $9, then find forms need $19, then find Stripe and custom forms need $49."
objections.answer: This is a fair reading of the plan structure and the honest answer is to pre-empt it rather than deny it: the gates are documented up front — signup forms require Pro Standard or higher, selling via form templates and custom/advanced forms require Pro Plus, framing requires Pro Plus — and the 7-day trial exists specifically to test the top features, named as custom domains and advanced forms, with no payment or credit card required. Plans can also be upgraded instantly at any time during or after the trial, and paid either as auto-renewing or pay-as-you-go.

objections.objection: "This is a one-page site. I could hand-write the HTML, or drop a template on Netlify or GitHub Pages, in an afternoon — and own it outright."
objections.answer: Partially answerable, and only for the parts that are genuinely annoying by hand: SSL on a custom domain is handled via Let's Encrypt, forms post to twenty named email platforms (ActiveCampaign, beehiiv, Brevo, Mailchimp, HubSpot, Klaviyo, Sendy and more) plus Stripe payments without writing or hosting a backend, and building can be started from a template with no signup required. For a reader who is genuinely comfortable writing HTML, the honest residual is the form backend and the certificate renewal, not the page itself — and Pro Plus lets them download the unminified sources if they later want to take it away.

objections.objection: "If I put a client's live site on a small indie product and it goes away or breaks, that's my reputation, not theirs. I don't know who runs this or whether it will be here next year."
objections.answer: The evidence does not answer this. There is nothing supplied on uptime, SLA, company size, ownership or longevity, and the only support statement is explicitly hedged — replies "usually within 24 hours" is not a guarantee. The genuine partial mitigations are exit routes rather than assurances: sites publish to a custom domain the buyer owns, so DNS can be repointed; sites can be transferred to another user; and Pro Plus can download the unminified HTML, CSS, JS and images. A dated changelog with activity through October 2026 shows the product is being worked on, but that is not a continuity promise and should not be dressed as one.

objections.objection: "Template sites look like template sites. My client will recognise it, or worse, their competitor will be running the same one."
objections.answer: Only partially answerable. The evidence covers the tells — branding can be removed from the footer, the site sits on the buyer's own domain, custom favicons and custom share images replace the defaults, premium templates are Pro-exclusive, and custom templates can be built and reused. What the evidence cannot show is design outcome or how any client actually perceived a finished site; there is no customer voice in the supplied material at all, so no claim about "nobody can tell" is supportable.

objections.objection: "I don't have the copy or the photos ready. Picking a tool isn't the blocker — finding the evening is."
objections.answer: The evidence supports a low-commitment first step rather than a solution to the underlying time problem: building can be started with no signup required, from dozens of templates grouped by what the page is for (Profile, Landing, Form, Portfolio, Sectioned) or from a blank page, and three sites can be published free, so there is no payment decision gating the first attempt. Nothing in the evidence quantifies how long a site takes to build, so the copy must not promise a number.

objections.objection: "Fifty client pages means paying for fifty sites, and the moment a client leaves I'm stuck hosting their page or rebuilding it for them."
objections.answer: Answerable from the plan structure: sites scale in one account rather than one subscription per site — 10 sites on Pro Standard at $19/year up to 50 at $69/year, 25 on Pro Plus at $49/year up to 50 at $89/year and beyond — and ownership of an individual site can be transferred to another Carrd user, with access to sites shareable with other users in the meantime.

objections.objection: "Adding a signup form means adding a cookie banner and another privacy thing I have to get right."
objections.answer: Partially answerable: Carrd's own analytics service is native and cookie-free with reporting in the dashboard, launched 2 October 2026, and third-party analytics is described as optional. On forms themselves the evidence only establishes that names and emails are captured to the buyer's chosen platform — it says nothing about consent handling or data processing terms, so that part stays unanswered.

objections.objection: "Annual billing on a card I'll forget about. I don't want another auto-renewal I have to hunt down in twelve months."
objections.answer: Directly answerable: plans can either auto-renew yearly or be paid as you go, whichever the buyer prefers, paid by PayPal or any major credit or debit card — and the 7-day trial requires no payment or credit card at all, so nothing is on file until the buyer decides.

rivals.name: Linktree
rivals.why: When the buyer just needs a single bio link listing a few destinations fast, this is the default they try before paying for a page they'd have to design themselves.

rivals.name: Webflow
rivals.why: If the one-pager needs to grow into a real multi-page site with custom interactions or a CMS later, this is where the buyer looks instead of outgrowing Carrd.

rivals.name: Framer
rivals.why: When the page needs to look like a premium, animated SaaS landing page rather than a simple static one-pager, the buyer compares this before settling for Carrd's simplicity.

rivals.name: Squarespace
rivals.why: The buyer or their business may already be paying for this as the full website/e-commerce platform, so a single Carrd page has to be justified as an addition rather than a replacement.

rivals.name: Wix
rivals.why: Many small businesses already have a Wix site running their main web presence, making it the incumbent a buyer has to decide whether to extend or bypass for a quick landing page.

rivals.name: Notion
rivals.why: Before paying for any page builder, many buyers just publish a public Notion page as their free, good-enough link-in-bio or landing page.
